title: Introduction to Hash Tables
description: Understand what hash tables are, how key-value pairs work, and why lookups are fast

blocks.text: One of the most powerful data structures you'll use. Hash tables let you store and retrieve data in O(1) no searching, no sorting required.
A hash table stores data as key → value pairs. You put something in using a key, and you get it back using that same key instantly.

Think of it like a coat check at a restaurant. You hand in your jacket, they give you a ticket number. When you want it back, you show the ticket no searching through every coat, just direct retrieval.
Under the hood, a hash table is just an array. The trick is a hash function it takes your key and converts it into an array index.

blocks.alt: Hash function maps a key to an array index

blocks.text: So when you write table["name"] = "Alice", the hash function decides which slot in the internal array to store it in. When you read it back, the same function runs again, lands on the same slot, and returns the value instantly.
Why O(1)? Because the hash function is just math it computes the index directly. No loops, no comparisons. One step to store, one step to retrieve.
Here is what the internal array looks like after inserting a few keys:

blocks.alt: Internal array of a hash table after inserting a few keys

blocks.text: Sometimes two different keys hash to the same index. This is called a collision.

blocks.alt: Two keys hashing to the same array index causing a collision

blocks.text: The most common fix is chaining each slot holds a list of all key-value pairs that landed there. When two keys collide, they just sit in the same list side by side.

A good hash function spreads keys evenly so collisions are rare. When there are few collisions, lookups stay O(1). If too many keys pile up in the same slot, it degrades to O(n) in the worst case but this is uncommon in practice.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Operation","Average","Worst case"],"rows":[["Insert key-value","O(1)","O(n)"],["Lookup by key","O(1)","O(n)"],["Delete by key","O(1)","O(n)"],["Check if key exists","O(1)","O(n)"]]}

blocks.text: The average case is almost always O(1). The worst case only happens when a bad hash function sends all keys to the same slot extremely rare with modern implementations.

codes.python:
scores = {}

# insert
scores["Alice"] = 95
scores["Bob"] = 82
scores["Carol"] = 78

# lookup
print(scores["Alice"])  # 95

# check if key exists
print("Bob" in scores)   # True
print("Dave" in scores)  # False

# delete
del scores["Bob"]

# loop over all pairs
for key, value in scores.items():
    print(f"{key}: {value}")

1. Frequency Count: Count how many times each element appears. The map stores element → count.
  2. Two Sum O(n) with a Map: Instead of checking every pair (O(n²)), store each number in a map as you go. For each new number, check if its complement already exists.
  3. Grouping / Bucketing: Use a map where the key is a category and the value is a list of items belonging to that category.

Remember: Hash tables are unordered they don't keep elements in insertion order in most languages (Python dicts do preserve order since 3.7, but HashMap in Java does not). 

If order matters, use a different structure.
